content: Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide used as a gastrointestinal agent, laxative, and hyperosmotic agent. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of constipation. The medication works by increasing the frequency of bowel movements and softening stools through its osmotic effects in the colon. Lactulose is poorly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract and is metabolized by colonic bacteria into lactic acid and small amounts of formic and acetic acids, which increase stool water content and acidify the colon. It typically takes 24 to 48 hours to produce a bowel movement. The standard adult dosage for constipation is 15 to 30 mL (10 to 20 g of lactulose) daily, which can be increased to 60 mL if necessary. Patients may find the solution more palatable when mixed with fruit juice, water, or milk. Pediatric dosing information is limited, and there is no FDA guidance for off-label uses in children or adults. Lactulose is contraindicated in patients requiring a low-galactose diet due to its galactose content. A theoretical risk exists for patients undergoing electrocautery procedures during proctoscopy or colonoscopy, as hydrogen gas accumulation in the colon could potentially lead to an explosive reaction. Although this has not been reported with lactulose, thorough bowel cleansing with a non-fermentable solution is recommended before such procedures. Adverse effects commonly include bloating, flatulence, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps. Excessive dosing may lead to dehydration, hypokalemia, and hypernatremia. Non-absorbable antacids may interfere with lactulose's efficacy by inhibiting the desired drop in colonic pH. Lactulose is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA, indicating no evidence of harm to the fetus in animal studies, though adequate human studies are lacking. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. It is unknown whether lactulose is excreted in human breast milk, so caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in geriatric, pediatric, or immunocompromised populations, nor in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. In cases of overdose, symptoms such as diarrhea and abdominal cramps are expected. Treatment involves discontinuing the medication. Lactulose is not well absorbed systemically, and less than 3% is excreted in the urine within 24 hours. Dialysis data for lactulose are unavailable, but its molecular similarity to sucrose suggests it may be dialyzable. Lactulose is supplied as a solution containing 670 mg/mL (10 g/15 mL) and is available in 237 mL (8 fl oz) and 946 mL (1 quart) bottles. The solution may darken over time due to its sugar content, but this does not affect its therapeutic efficacy. Patients should be advised to contact their healthcare provider if unusual diarrhea occurs. There is no established interaction between lactulose and alcohol, but patients should consult their physician regarding alcohol consumption while on this medication. Lactulose is marketed under various brand names, including Kristalose®, Cholac®, Constilac®, Constulose®, Generlac®, and Enulose®.
